status_note: Originally scheduled for early November 2015 and postponed: the Superpark opened on 24 October but snow was insufficient to build a compliant World Snowboard Tour International setup.
notes: First tour stop of the World Snowboard Tour northern-hemisphere season and of the QParks Snowboard Tour; contested on a pro kicker line.
Opening stop of the 2016/17 QParks Snowboard Tour.

Seventh season, EUR 40,000 total prize money. Ten stops: Pleasure Jam, Superpark Dachstein (19 Nov 2016); Battle ROJal, Snowpark Schoeneben (7 Jan 2017); Penken Battle, Vans Penken Park (14 Jan); Blue Tomato Plan P, Superpark Planai (28 Jan); Nock'n'Rock, Snowpark Turracher Hoehe (11 Feb); Sick Trick Tour Open, Snowpark Kitzbuehel (18 Feb); Gold & Glory Golden, Roofpark Axamer Lizum (25 Feb); Oakley Schilthorn Open, Skyline Snowpark Schilthorn (11 Mar); Shred Masters Feldberg, Badenova Snowpark Feldberg (18 Mar); Roof Battle, Superpark Dachstein (22 Apr). Covers Austria, Germany, Italy and Switzerland.
Six divisions, each capped at 25 riders; fastest of two runs, second run as tiebreaker.

city: Farellones / Lo Barnechea, Santiago Metropolitan Region
notes: Eighth edition and the first to count for the WSF South America Tour. WSF/TTR 2-Star slopestyle, USD 3,000 prize money, around 80 professional athletes from Chile, Argentina, Brazil, Spain, the USA and Canada.

city: Farellones / Lo Barnechea, Santiago Metropolitan Region
notes: USD 8,000 in prizes; open to skiers as well as snowboarders. Described by the WSF as taking place in the best terrain park in South America.

Wikipedia gives Kaprun; the WSF's provisional 06/07 women's tour calendar, published 24 October 2006, listed the European Roxy Chicken Jam at St Moritz, Switzerland. The two sources disagree on venue.
The season-defining event of the 2006/07 TTR women's tour, where the women's TTR world champion was decided.
Second Roxy Chicken Jam of the 2007 calendar year; opens the 2007/08 women's season.
Wikipedia records a projected purse of over USD 150,000 for the 2008 US event, one of the largest in women's snowboarding at the time. Exact dates not given.
Inaugural edition, founded by Brendan O'Dowd and Patryck Bernier. Reported 6,000 spectators and a $10,000 winner-take-all purse.
SnowboardQuebec's provincial history records Guillaume Brochu as the 2003 winner (not recorded as a result row in this wave).
SnowboardQuebec records Matt Dano as the 2005 winner (not recorded as a result row in this wave).
Sebastien Toutant, aged 13, was moved up from the amateur division and won the pro category in his first major contest.
SnowboardQuebec records Charles Reid as the 2008 winner (not recorded as a result row in this wave). Last edition under Empire title sponsorship.
First year with Ride Snowboards as title sponsor. SnowboardQuebec records Sebastien Toutant winning for a second time, aged 16 (not recorded as a result row in this wave).
First year the series ran a US stop as well, at Snoqualmie, Washington on 12-13 March 2010.
Series ran stops in Germany, the USA and Canada this year; Canadian dates not given in the source. SnowboardQuebec records Sebastien Toutant winning a third time.

Last edition listed by the event's own edition table. SnowboardQuebec's timeline places a cancelled Shakedown season in its 2015 entry, and CBC reported a Shakedown cancellation in January 2016 for lack of sponsorship and snow; whether the 2015 contest ran and the 2016 one was cancelled is unresolved - see open questions.

Whistler Blackcomb's 60th anniversary timeline dates the first Showcase Showdown to 1 February 1997. Snowboard Magazine's billing of the 2015 event as the 18th annual implies a 1998 start instead; the discrepancy is unresolved. The Whistler Museum separately records a Showcase Snowboards halfpipe competition on Blackcomb in 1992, won in the male 18-plus category by Whistler's Robin Dow, which may be a predecessor.

Big air with a junior rail jam added for the first time. $22,000 in total prizes; $10,000 to the pro men's winner plus a start in the WSSF Monster Energy Shred Show. Presented by Monster Energy, Burton and Vans, with an after-party featuring Anti-Flag. Snowboard Magazine lists the contest date as Saturday 14 March; the Georgia Straight gives 14-15 March.
Dates from a third-party events roundup, not from the organiser.

edition_label: 1985 Snoboard Shop North American Snowboarding Championships (first edition)
notes: SnowboardQuebec's history page states Ken Achenbach's Snoboard Shop launched the North American Snowboarding Championships in Alberta in 1985 with a $20,000 purse, calling it the first snowboard event held in Canada, and says the series ended in 1988. Venue for 1985 is unconfirmed: the 1987 edition is sourced to Sunshine Village and later accounts describe an annual May long weekend contest there, but the one source naming a 1985 result places the event 'in Calgary'.

Held on the May long weekend with a $20,000 purse. A photograph of Dave Achenbach from this event ran on the cover of the first issue of TransWorld Snowboarding. Exact dates and the disciplines run were not sourced.

edition_label: 1988 Snoboard Shop North American Snowboarding Championships
status_note: Venue changed: Sunshine Village withdrew from hosting mid-season and Mt Norquay took the event on.
notes: Norquay's own history says hosting the event put the resort on the cover of TransWorld Snowboarding. SnowboardQuebec's history records 1988 as the final year of the series.

edition_label: 2013 Snowboard Jamboree / FIS Snowboarding World Championships
disciplines: big-air | halfpipe | slopestyle | boardercross | parallel-giant-slalom | parallel-slalom
notes: The 2013 FIS Snowboarding World Championships were staged at Stoneham on these dates. Ski Canada's 2014 preview describes the 2014 Jamboree as the 9th edition, which places the 2013 festival as the 8th.

venue: Stoneham Mountain Resort and Quebec City
notes: Billed as the 9th Snowboard Jamboree and the 15th World Cup held in Quebec. First year the event was sanctioned as a 5-star World Snowboard Tour stop and first year it offered three freestyle World Cup disciplines. Last international snowboard competition before the Sochi 2014 Olympics. Stairsmasters video contest returned.

venue: Stoneham Mountain Resort and Ilot Fleurie, Quebec City
status_note: The halfpipe World Cup scheduled for 22 February at Stoneham was cancelled: organisers cited a significant lack of snow, warm weather and a labour dispute making an FIS-standard pipe impossible.
notes: 10th edition and the 16th FIS Snowboard World Cup held at the festival. Big air on 20 February at Ilot Fleurie in downtown Quebec City, slopestyle on 21 February at Stoneham. About 200 athletes from more than 20 countries. First time 19 women contested big air at a World Cup here. Stairsmasters video contest ran alongside.

Moved entirely into downtown Quebec City and cut back to a single big air World Cup, carrying both FIS and TTR World Snowboard Tour points. Maxence Parrot worked on the venue build. Programme also included the Stairsmasters video contest and the IF3 film festival. Organisers described 16 years of World Cup racing in the region and seven consecutive World Cups in Quebec City from 2009.

edition_label: 2018 Jamboree Big Air World Cup Finals
notes: Listed on Canada Snowboard's 2017-18 domestic calendar as the Jamboree Big Air World Cup Finals.

edition_label: 2019 Jamboree Snowboard and Ski Big Air
notes: Listed on Canada Snowboard's 2018-19 domestic calendar as the Jamboree Snowboard and Ski Big Air.

venue: Yamabiko B Course, Nozawa Onsen Ski Resort
status_note: Run as a banked slalom rather than SBM's usual freeride-performance and obstacle-slalom format, because seasonal conditions made it impossible to prepare the standard courses.
notes: Open practice Friday 29 March, competition Saturday 30 March. 150 men and 100 women; entrants had to be 18 or over and resident in Japan. Entry JPY 2,000, JPY 1,000 for JSBA/PSA members.

Snowboarder/TransWorld 1990s timeline: the Victoria World Cup Japan at Rusutsu, with over one million dollars spent, was 'the richest contest so far'. No dates, format or podium given. This is a single tour stop, not a full season row.

status_note: Saturday's main contest was postponed because of weather and replaced by a Best Trick Session on the last three obstacles.
notes: Sunday ran as the TTR 3-Star event with qualification runs and finals; skate sessions and a party ran alongside.

WSF Elite Level Event counting for the World Snowboard Points List, EUR 65,000 prize purse. Riders had several days to film single-take runs with follow-cam filmers (no editing permitted), judged afterwards by an international WSF panel. Snowboard slopestyle on the Absolut Park kicker line; Best Trick Rail open to snowboarders and freeskiers in a dedicated jib park. Award ceremony 14 March at Haus Flachau.
Swatch TTR 3-Star. Ran the week after the Garnier Fructis Australian Open at Perisher Blue.
Billed by the WSF as Australia's biggest Swatch TTR tour event (4-Star), drawing riders from across the southern hemisphere.

status_note: Slopestyle scaled back from three days to two.
notes: 25 riders. A '28 Stairs' rail jam ran alongside. Scotty James, then 17, led after day one; Gjermund Braaten withdrew injured. The WSF report is dated 23 August 2011 and does not name the resort.
Also referred to as the Mike Baker Banked Slalom. Dates from a third-party events roundup.

Four stops: Vuokatti (7-8 Feb), Ounasvaara (21-22 Feb), Talma (14-15 Mar) and Ruka (9-12 Apr, run as SM15, the Finnish championships). Grom, Rookie and Open categories; EUR 35 entry with an FSA licence covering the three regional events; Burton Riglet park and coaching for parents and non-competing young riders.
Closing event of the Swiss-Ski Audi Snowboard Series season, and the first time in years that the snowboard freestyle championships were held together with the freeskiers.
Listed by the WSF as Japan's banked slalom, roughly 1.5 hours from Tokyo. Earliest edition found.
WSF report says the contest had run for three seasons before this one. Organised by former pro rider Yosuke Nishida, director of the TJ brand, on Mt Tanigawa.

Heats on 5 March in clear weather, finals over two runs on 6 March. Course deliberately balanced for regular and goofy riders; based out of the Canyons lodge at the resort base. Snowboard brands demoed 2016/17 models alongside.
Over 400 people across the two days. Opened with a traditional ceremony praying for safety, reflecting the mountain's avalanche history. Riders received a TBS x Volcom collaboration T-shirt.

Pilot project: Terje Haakonsen, Daniel Franck and Oakley invited 12 riders to Norway to test the concept. Halfpipe in Trysil, surfing and freeriding in Lofoten. Terje later described 2014 as '15 years since we did the pilot event'.
First full competition: halfpipe, quarterpipe, surf, skate and freeride.
Moved south because of weather: halfpipe at Hemsedal, quarterpipe at Holmenkollen in Oslo. Heikki Sorsa set a 9.3 m quarterpipe air record at this event.

status_note: Cancelled after the sports marketing firm Sportsworld went bankrupt; Terje Haakonsen personally took on the financial obligations.

notes: Halfpipe and quarterpipe plus a music and lifestyle programme.

status_note: Arctic storms forced relocations; the halfpipe and slopestyle were cancelled and only the Tromsø quarterpipe ran, in pouring rain.
notes: Last edition held above the Arctic Circle; from 2006 the event moved to the Oslo area. Show sessions replaced the cancelled contests.

status_note: Major weather delays; scaffolding had to be replaced before the event.
notes: First edition in Oslo.

Terje Haakonsen set a quarterpipe air record of 9.8 m above the lip, beating Heikki Sorsa's 9.3 m from 2001. Venue not stated in the sources I opened. [QA-corrected: venue and date taken from the cited the-house.com history, which the original row overlooked.]
About 7,000 spectators in good weather.

TTR 6Star slopestyle. Practice and a downtown Oslo grand opening on Thursday 4 March, semi-finals Saturday 6 March, finals Sunday 7 March; capacity 4,000. Course shaper Claes Hoegstrom. Peetu Piiroinen's win here secured the Swatch TTR world title.

6Star slopestyle with 30 men and 16 women and a USD 100,000 purse; qualification from the TTR ranking (top 20 men, top 10 women after the Burton European Open), qualifying events and wildcards. Staged as the trial run for the 2012 World Snowboarding Championships.
Main snowboard event on 9 March 2013, with a halfpipe competition (snowboard and freestyle ski) five days earlier; the volunteer call covered 6-13 March. Start date not stated explicitly.

Rider-designed format: 12 riders arrived 11 March and had the pipe from 12-15 March to decide the arena and contest format themselves, with the public event on Saturday 15 March. Judged on skill, amplitude and creativity rather than a standard run score. 15 years after the 1999 pilot.

20th birthday edition, billed by the WSF as Europe's longest established winter snowsports festival. Hosted the British Snowboard and Freeski Championships across kids, rookie, pro and Olympian fields; a skiercross ran alongside.
First return to Scotland in 32 years. Ran as the TSA British Snowboard Championships alongside the Ellis Brigham British Freeski Championships. Cairngorm built the first British halfpipe in 1991.
Inaugural edition. Editions were normally held around 11 February.
Olympic year; the Japanese Wikipedia notes that in Olympic years the date shifted to late January or late February.
Olympic year.
The Makomanai open-air stadium carried the Sekisui Heim naming rights from 2007.
Olympic year.
Last edition held outdoors at Makomanai.
Moved indoors to the Sapporo Dome as a 'full model change', with a 36 m temporary in-run scaffold.

Final edition. The organising office announced on 30 September 2014 that the event would not continue. Date of 23 February 2014 taken from the English Wikipedia article; the Japanese article gives no per-edition dates.

First TTR season: nine events worldwide with the Arctic Challenge as the final stop, each event awarding one TTR Medallion and an Arctic Challenge invite. No women's tour until 2005/06. Events: Nissan X-Trail Jam, Nokia Air & Style, O'Neill SB Jam, Burton European Open, Champs Open, Vans Triple Crown of Snowboarding, The Battle, Quiksilver Slopestyle Pro, US Open.
Same nine events as the previous season; the nine TTR medallion winners were invited to the Arctic Challenge, again the tour final.

Season edition rows use the calendar year the season ended. The Arctic Challenge's own 2005 site published the 2004/2005 TTR Tour standings, with Andy Finch as overall champion, which confirms the season ran.

Introduction of the 1-6Star tier system, the TTR ranking system, the first TTR website (ttrworldtour.com) and the official Women's Tour. 67 events in total. The TTR World Ranking list launched 5 December 2005 and the first-ever TTR World Tour Champions were crowned at the US Open.

First season with a dedicated women's tour, announced 24 October 2006. WSF described a provisional women's calendar of over 20 events offering more than 30 possible results, kicking off with the Burton Abominable Snow Jam at Mt Hood in July 2006 and ending at the Roxy Chicken Jam Finals in Park City, 22-25 March 2007. The Billabong Pro Junior in Australia and the Burton Australian Open were cancelled for poor snow.

edition_label: 2007/08 Swatch TTR World Snowboard Tour season
notes: Introduction of a $250,000 end-of-season prize purse. 176 results registered across four formats from events in 27 nations; 3,417 riders (2,706 men, 711 women) from 41 nations ranked.

edition_label: 2008/09 Swatch TTR World Snowboard Tour season
notes: First of Peetu Piiroinen's three consecutive men's overall titles, per Guinness World Records.

edition_label: 2009/10 Swatch TTR World Snowboard Tour season
notes: Second of Peetu Piiroinen's three consecutive men's overall titles; WSF reported he secured the Swatch TTR world title by winning the Oakley Arctic Challenge in March 2010.

edition_label: 2010/11 Swatch TTR World Snowboard Tour season
notes: Third of Peetu Piiroinen's three consecutive men's overall titles, per Guinness World Records.

TTR's 10th anniversary season. Highlight was the inaugural World Snowboarding Championships at Oslo Vinterpark in February 2012, developed and owned by TTR and the World Snowboard Federation and run as a 6Star tour event - the first world championships organised by snowboarders since 1999. The Burton European Open was postponed to March, making WCS qualification difficult.

First season under the new name. TTR announced on 2-4 July 2012 that the TTR World Tour would be called the World Snowboard Tour from the 2012/13 season; TTR president Reto Lamm said the tour then covered around 350 events across five continents. Headline events named in the announcement were Air & Style Beijing and Innsbruck, Burton European and US Open, O'Neill Evolution Davos and The Arctic Challenge Oslo.
Season in which the six star tiers were replaced by four event categories: Regional, National, International and Elite.

First season under the new tour concept agreed at the May 2014 General Assembly in Barcelona: six star tiers replaced by four categories (Regional, National, International, Elite), with the Elite events forming the WST Pro Series. Titles were awarded in slopestyle and halfpipe only, at the Burton US Open on 8 March 2015.

status_note: Final season before the tour brand was retired.
notes: TTR Pro Snowboarding restricted access to the World Snowboard Points List in January 2017 to force the snowboard industry to fund it. The merger with the WSF was announced 25 May 2017; from the 2017/18 season the merged organisation offered direct membership and the World Snowboard Tour brand ceased to exist.

Organised by Paul Graves. Doug Bouton won. Burton's own history page opens the US Open lineage with this event; the PSIA-AASI archive treats it as a separate contest from the National Snowboarding Championships Jake Burton Carpenter organised at Snow Valley the following year. Recorded here as the first row of the lineage with the dispute unresolved.

No lift access; competitors hiked the hill. Andy Coghlan won men's slalom and downhill. Several sources describe this, not 1982, as the first edition of what became the US Open, and Burton's own later edition numbering (2002 = 20th, 2009 = 27th, 2012 = 30th, 2020 = 38th) counts from 1983.
Final year at Snow Valley. Andy Coghlan repeated in slalom and downhill.

First year at Stratton Mountain and the year the event was formally called the US Open Snowboarding Championships. Riders began wearing speed suits. Tom Sims won men's slalom; Andy Coghlan defended the downhill.
Over 200 competitors in the pre-qualifiers. Andy Coghlan won slalom and downhill again.
Craig Kelly won the men's slalom.
Halfpipe debuted at the US Open and was immediately treated as the benchmark for competition pipes. Craig Kelly took the overall title. An ice storm preceded the event.

Last year the downhill was run. Craig Kelly won the Overall title. [QA-corrected: the cited sources say halfpipe DEBUTED at the 1989 US Open and that Kelly took the Overall title; the earlier claim of a second consecutive halfpipe title was unsupported. The downhill discipline was uncited and has been removed.]
Terje Haakonsen's US Open halfpipe debut. Craig Kelly won, against a field including Shaun Palmer and Jeff Brushie.
Crowd and competitor numbers roughly doubled. Inverts ridden in competition for the first time. Janna Meyen won the women's halfpipe over Tina Basich.
Terje Haakonsen won the men's halfpipe; Tricia Byrnes won the women's.
Fresh snow and clear skies. Terje Haakonsen took a second consecutive halfpipe title on his new Burton pro model.
Shannon Dunn and Todd Richards won the halfpipes. Terje Haakonsen sat out with an ankle injury.

Big air debuted at the US Open. Terje Haakonsen won a third halfpipe title. Victoria Jealouse won the women's super-G, recorded here as discipline 'other' because super-G is not in the Linestry discipline vocabulary.
Held in the season snowboarding's inclusion in the 1998 Nagano Olympics was announced. Peter Line and Cara-Beth Burnside won big air; Jimi Scott and Satu Jarvela won halfpipe.
Reported crowd of over 10,000 for the halfpipe. Todd Richards edged Terje Haakonsen; Barrett Christy won the women's pipe.

Remembered as 'the Year of the Mist' for heavy fog. Boardercross debuted. Rob Kingwill won the men's halfpipe; Nicola Thost, the 1998 Olympic champion, won the women's. Mike Michalchuk's back-to-back 1620s are cited by Burton as an early double-cork-era moment.
Ross Powers won the men's halfpipe with McTwists and 900s; Nicola Thost won the women's for a second consecutive year.

First superpipe at the US Open, reported as roughly 300 feet long with 15-foot walls. Guillaume Morisset and Natasza Zurek won for Canada. Recorded as halfpipe; the pipe event was run as a superpipe from this year.
Danny Kass won the men's halfpipe, narrowly over Vermont's Abe Teter. Natasza Zurek took a second consecutive women's title.

Held a month after the Salt Lake City Olympics, with a reported 30,000-plus spectators. Kelly Clark won quarterpipe and halfpipe; Danny Kass defended the men's halfpipe. First Tracks called it the 20th year of the competition, which counts from 1983. [v0.2: MountainZone reports the first US Open slopestyle finals on 17 March 2002, with both podiums; discipline list corrected.]

First rail jam at the US Open, won by Travis Rice; first live television broadcast; Philips became the first title sponsor. Ross Powers won the halfpipe, Gretchen Bleiler the women's, Shaun White the slopestyle. MountainZone's contemporaneous slopestyle report is dated 2003-03-15; full event dates not sourced. The usopen03 schedule page confirms Rail Jam final Friday 14 March, halfpipe finals Saturday 15 March, slopestyle finals Sunday 16 March.]

Women rode the rail jam for the first time; Leanne Pelosi won. Danny Kass won the halfpipe and the overall title; Kelly Clark won the women's halfpipe. Priscilla Levac and Jake Blauvelt won slopestyle. [v0.3 archive: 2004 Open Championships of Snowboarding calendar: "Philips US Open March 16-21, 2004 Stratton, VT USA".] [v0.3 archive: 2004 Open Championships of Snowboarding calendar: "Philips US Open March 16-21, 2004 Stratton, VT USA".]

Danny Kass became the first rider to win four US Open halfpipe titles. Janna Meyen won her first title since 1991. Shaun White won halfpipe and slopestyle. The quarterpipe was revived, won by Danny Davis and Hana Beaman. White and Beaman took Most Valuable Rider awards. Marked by Burton as the 25th anniversary. Shaun White and Torah Bright won the first Burton Global Open Series championship titles, USD 100,000 each. Kelly Clark won a third halfpipe title; Travis Rice and Jamie Anderson won slopestyle. Total prize purse reported at USD 471,500. Rated 6Star on the Swatch TTR World Snowboard Tour. Slopestyle finals ran 2008-03-21 (Shaun White and Kjersti Buaas) with halfpipe finals the following day; the event's start date was not sourced. Cheryl Maas and Tim Humphreys won big air.

Closing event of the 2008/09 Burton Global Open Series; dates as announced in the series calendar. AlpineZone called it the 27th US Open. Danny Kass won a record fifth halfpipe title; Torah Bright won a third. Chas Guldemond and Kjersti Buaas won slopestyle. A best trick contest and a junior jam were also run, recorded as 'other'.

Halfpipe finals ran 2010-03-20 in a slushy pipe; full event dates not sourced. Kazuhiro Kokubo won his first halfpipe title and Kelly Clark became the first woman to win four. Kazuhiro Kokubo won a second consecutive halfpipe title and dedicated it to tsunami-hit Japan. Kelly Clark won a fifth consecutive halfpipe title and her first Burton Global Open Series championship. Eric Willett and Enni Rukajarvi won their first slopestyle titles.

Last US Open at Stratton after 28 editions there. Hit by a freak snowstorm. Shaun White won halfpipe; Elena Hight ended Kelly Clark's streak; Seb Toots and Jamie Anderson won slopestyle; Chas Guldemond and Kjersti Buaas won The Jam. A veterans' race, the Washed Up Cup, was run on the Friday night.

First US Open at Vail after 28 years in Vermont. Over USD 340,000 in prize money. Mark McMorris won his first slopestyle title, Spencer O'Brien the women's; Shaun White won the halfpipe with 14-year-old Ayumu Hirano second.
Slopestyle finals 2014-03-07, halfpipe finals 2014-03-08. Mark McMorris won a second consecutive slopestyle; Jamie Anderson won the women's; Kelly Clark won the halfpipe.

Yuki Kadono won men's slopestyle with back-to-back triple cork 1620s, reported as a competition first. Jamie Anderson won a fourth slopestyle title; Kelly Clark won an eighth halfpipe title; Taku Hiraoka won the men's halfpipe.

USD 343,000 prize purse. Shaun White returned to the halfpipe podium; 15-year-old Chloe Kim won her first halfpipe title. Jamie Anderson and Kyle Mack won slopestyle. Junior jam halfpipe on 2016-03-01.
Anna Gasser won her first title in women's slopestyle; Mark McMorris won the men's. Shaun White and Chloe Kim defended their halfpipe titles. Junior jam halfpipe for riders 14 and under.
First post-PyeongChang edition. Zoi Sadowski-Synnott and Red Gerard won slopestyle; Maddie Mastro and Scotty James won halfpipe.
Halfpipe and slopestyle for men and women plus a junior jam for riders under 15.

The last US Open held. Run about four months after Jake Burton Carpenter's death and dedicated to him. USD 373,000 prize purse. Junior jam halfpipe 2020-02-25; slopestyle finals 2020-02-28; halfpipe finals 2020-02-29.

status_note: Cancelled; the event did not return to Vail afterwards.
notes: Scheduled for 2021-03-01 to 2021-03-06 and cancelled. edition_label: 10th Vans Waengl Taengl presented by G-SHOCK

notes: The crew said they would instead focus on youth development and new event formats.

First edition. Run inside the 1997 World Ski & Snowboard Festival (4-13 April 1997). Over 8,000 spectators at the base of Whistler Mountain. Exact contest date not sourced.
Final edition. Moved out of the World Ski & Snowboard Festival to the May long weekend. Reported in 2001 by Pique Newsmagazine as the last running.

status_note: Not held. WestBeach Sports redirected its funding to sponsor the World Snowboarding Championship instead; company president Steve Dewar told Pique the brand opportunity was 'too good to pass up'.
notes: The Masters Group organised both the WestBeach Classic and the World Snowboarding Championship.

Pique Newsmagazine's 2001 year in sports records snowboard cross, two halfpipes, alpine and big air over these dates, with Guillaume Morisset taking a bronze, Natasza Zurek a silver and Jasey-Jay Anderson a silver in parallel giant slalom. Belongs to the 2001-02 season.

notes: Announced by Canada Snowboard in November 2018 and listed on its 2018-19 domestic calendar.

The first snowboard halfpipe contest. Organised by Tom Sims with Mike Chantry; the pipe was pushed up with a snowcat and then dug out by hand. Riders on Jake Burton's East Coast team objected to counting halfpipe in the overall standings and reportedly threatened a boycott. No exact date found in any source opened; Sims' USPTO service-mark registration claims first use in commerce on 15 February 1983, which is the closest thing to a contemporaneous date. CONFLICT: a 2014 Snowboard Magazine piece on the Sims Retro World Championships refers to 'the 1982 2nd World Snowboard Championships in Soda Springs', implying a 1981 or 1982 first edition; every other source opened calls 1983 the inaugural year.

Tahoe Quarterly states Terry Kidwell won the halfpipe at Soda Springs in 1984 and 1985; the Sierra Sun halfpipe history says Kidwell 'won the following two years' after Eddie Hargraves' 1983 win. No date, no full podium and no other disciplines confirmed.

Second of Terry Kidwell's two Soda Springs halfpipe wins per Tahoe Quarterly. Note that Breckenridge's own history page claims Breckenridge 'hosts the first snowboard World Cup' in 1985 - a different event from this championship, and itself disputed (see open questions).

First Breckenridge edition, March 1986, on a hand-dug halfpipe on Peak 9. Breckenridge had lifted its snowboarding ban in 1984, the first major Colorado resort to do so. Paul Alden persuaded Breckenridge management to accept the halfpipe as a legitimate competitive format; Swatch was a major sponsor and the event drew national media. Greg Stump filmed it for 'Maltese Flamingo' (1986). Terry Kidwell is reported to have won the halfpipe again in 1986 after the championships moved to Colorado (Tahoe Quarterly) - treated here as unconfirmed, no result row written. No full podium found in any source opened. Sources give only the month, not the days.

DATE CONFLICT. The Snowboarder/TransWorld 1980s timeline and Paul Alden's obituaries put the second Breckenridge Worlds in March 1987 - specifically, NASBA was formed on 8 March 1987, 'the day after' the championships ended, which implies the event finished 7 March 1987. TransWorld's halfpipe history instead dates the 1987 Breckenridge World Championships to 2-5 April 1987 and calls its pipe (about 200 feet long with near-vertical six-foot walls) the best in snowboarding to that point. Dates left null. Jose Fernandes is reported to have won the giant slalom on an asymmetrical board (snowboarding8090.com) - not corroborated, no result row written. Craig Kelly's published timeline lists 'Swatch World Championships' results for 1987 and 1988, which is the strongest indication that the Breckenridge Worlds carried Swatch's name.
